patient.name: Winston Baptiste
patient.complaint: Two weeks of severe mid-back pain at night, now weak legs and unable to pass urine
background: Prostate cancer with bone metastases, on hormone therapy
Retired electrician from Brixton, lives with his daughter
Walked independently with a stick until last week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'Which is the most important diagnosis to exclude?' in a patient with known cancer, back pain and new leg weakness or retention. The UMN versus LMN pattern separates cord compression from cauda equina.

points: Two weeks of severe **mid-back pain**, worst at night.
Pain wraps round his chest like a **band**.
Legs feel heavy for 3 days; stumbling at home.
Has not passed urine for 10 hours.

steps.lead: Prostate cancer is one of the four primaries (**prostate, breast, lung, myeloma**) behind metastatic cord compression, and Winston already has bone metastases.
Winston's **nocturnal thoracic pain** came first; the leg weakness and retention are the red flags that make this an emergency.

steps.text: Back pain for two weeks, then **progressive bilateral weakness**: the window to save function is closing.

points: Both legs: **increased tone**, brisk knee and ankle reflexes.
Tender over the T9 spinous process.
Bladder palpable to just below the umbilicus.

visual.title: Where the swelling is
visual.caption: A palpable, dull bladder rising to near the umbilicus: painless **urinary retention** from cord compression.

steps.lead: Brisk reflexes, extensor plantars and a sensory level at T10: Winston has **UMN signs** below a thoracic lesion, well above L1.

steps.q: Which pattern fits a lesion compressing Winston's cord at T9?
steps.r: Cord compression above L1 gives **UMN signs** below it. Flaccid, areflexic legs with saddle anaesthesia suggest cauda equina.

steps.lead: Without urgent treatment Winston risks **permanent paraplegia** and lifelong bladder and bowel dysfunction.

steps.title: Cord compression vs conus vs cauda equina
head: Feature
Cord compression (above L1)
Conus medullaris (L1)
Cauda equina (below L1)

steps.lead: Winston's UMN signs point away from **cauda equina** or a disc; an epidural haematoma would need anticoagulation or a recent epidural.

steps.text: Back pain in a patient with **known cancer** is metastatic cord compression until proven otherwise, even before any weakness. Do not call it 'mechanical'.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' with MRI whole spine as the answer, done within 24 hours. In suspected MSCC, the trap is that dexamethasone comes before the scan.

steps.q: Winston's MRI is 3 hours away. What should happen now?
steps.r: In suspected MSCC, **dexamethasone is given first**, before investigations. Waiting allows irreversible damage.

steps.lead: Winston has his **dexamethasone 16 mg** in ED before he goes to the scanner.
Winston has an **MRI of the whole spine**, not just the painful level, because metastases are often at more than one level.

visual.title: Time from suspicion to MRI whole spine
visual.label: Winston 4 h
visual.caption: With neurological signs, the MRI should be immediate and always **within 24 hours**.

points: MRI: **T9 vertebral body metastasis** with epidural extension.
Spinal cord compressed with high signal (oedema).
Smaller metastases at L2 and L4, no compression there.

steps.title: Bloods
steps.text: High ALP and calcium fit **bone metastases**; a normal-ish CRP makes an epidural abscess unlikely.

steps.title: Suspected MSCC pathway
nodes: MRI whole spine within 24 h (CT if MRI not possible)
Refer: acute oncology and spinal surgery

steps.text: Do not order an MRI of only the lumbar spine because the leg is weak. Thoracic lesions cause leg signs and MSCC is often **multilevel**: scan the **whole spine**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': dexamethasone 16 mg STAT with a PPI, then surgical decompression or radiotherapy, with urgent acute oncology/spinal referral.

steps.lead: Winston gets **dexamethasone 16 mg STAT**, then **8 mg BD**, plus **omeprazole** to protect his stomach.

steps.q: Why does Winston need a PPI alongside dexamethasone?
steps.r: High-dose steroids raise the risk of **peptic ulceration**; a PPI protects against it.

steps.lead: Winston is referred straight to **acute oncology and the spinal surgeons**; this is a same-day emergency.

points: Spinal surgeons review: fit for surgery, single compressing level.
Decompression and stabilisation planned for the morning.

steps.lead: Winston is fit, so **surgical decompression** is definitive; **radiotherapy** would be the choice if he could not have surgery.

steps.title: Managing MSCC
nodes: Dexamethasone 16 mg STAT, then 8 mg BD + PPI

steps.text: Function at treatment predicts outcome: patients who **walk in** usually walk out. Speed is everything: steroids, scan and referral the same day.

steps.lead: Even with treatment, Winston may be left with **bladder dysfunction**, reduced mobility or neuropathic pain, so early rehab is planned.
Winston's care follows **NICE CG75**: suspected MSCC means MRI whole spine within 24 hours and an immediate call to acute oncology.

science.exam: Science questions ask why compression above L1 gives UMN signs while cauda equina gives LMN signs, and why steroids or speed matter.

steps.lead: The T9 metastasis squeezes **corticospinal tract** fibres heading to Winston's legs, so he has UMN signs below T9.
Had Winston's lesion been below L1, it would hit **nerve roots**, giving floppy, areflexic legs and saddle anaesthesia.

visual.title: Level of the lesion
visual.label: Winston T9
visual.caption: Above the conus (about L1) = cord = UMN. Below = roots = LMN.

steps.q: A lesion at L4 compressing the cauda equina causes which sign?
steps.r: Cauda equina is **nerve roots**: LMN signs, so reflexes are reduced or absent.

steps.lead: Winston's prostate cancer seeded his **T9 vertebral body**; epidural tumour plus oedema compressed the cord, and the oedema part is steroid-responsive.
An epidural bleed fills a **closed canal** fast, so pressure climbs within hours; that is why it needs emergency evacuation.
Every hour Winston waited risked **ischaemic cord injury** that steroids and surgery cannot reverse.

mcq.q: What is the earliest and most common symptom of spinal cord compression?
mcq.r: **Back pain**, classically nocturnal and mid-thoracic, comes first.

mcq.q: Which four primaries most commonly cause metastatic cord compression?
Which signs does cord compression above L1 produce below the lesion?
mcq.r: **UMN signs**: hyperreflexia, spasticity, extensor plantars and a sensory level.

mcq.q: Which feature most suggests cauda equina syndrome?
mcq.r: Cauda equina: **saddle anaesthesia**, retention, reduced anal tone, bilateral sciatica (LMN).

mcq.q: Between which levels do most disc herniations occur?
What is the first-line investigation for suspected cord compression?
In suspected MSCC, what should be given before imaging?
What is the dexamethasone regimen for suspected MSCC?
mcq.r: **16 mg STAT, then 8 mg BD**, with a PPI.

mcq.q: Which definitive treatment is used if the patient cannot have surgery?
mcq.r: **Radiotherapy** if surgical decompression is not possible.

mcq.q: Why does cauda equina syndrome cause LMN signs?
o: It compresses nerve roots, not the cord
It is always caused by infection
mcq.r: The cauda equina is **lumbosacral nerve roots** (peripheral nerves) below the conus.

prompts.q: What is spinal cord compression and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: in a cancer patient it is metastatic until proven otherwise.

points.p: Compression of the cord (or cauda equina) causing dysfunction below the lesion
points.why: Can cause permanent paralysis and sphincter loss.

points.p: Metastatic spinal cord compression
points.why: The commonest exam cause.

points.p: Disc prolapse
points.why: Majority of herniations are at L5/S1.

points.p: Epidural abscess
points.why: Fever, IVDU, raised CRP.

points.p: Trauma, vertebral collapse, epidural haematoma
points.why: Haematoma: anticoagulants or epidurals.

prompts.q: Which primary cancers most often cause metastatic cord compression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three solid tumours plus one blood cancer.

points.p: Prostate
points.why: Classic exam stem: elderly man with bone metastases.

points.p: Breast
points.why: Can present years after the original cancer.

points.p: Lung
points.why: Can be the first presentation of lung cancer.

points.p: Myeloma
points.why: Look for anaemia, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment.

prompts.q: What are the symptoms and red flags of spinal cord compression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: back pain first, then legs, then bladder.

points.p: Back pain: earliest and commonest, nocturnal, thoracic, worse lying down
points.why: Severe unremitting thoracic pain disturbing sleep is a red flag.

points.p: Radicular or band-like pain
points.why: Follows a dermatome round the chest.

points.p: Leg weakness, gait difficulty, sensory disturbance
points.why: Progressive weakness means urgent action.

points.p: Urinary retention, faecal incontinence or constipation
points.why: Sphincter involvement is a late, bad sign.

points.p: Localised spinal tenderness
points.why: Points to the level of the lesion.

prompts.q: What examination signs does cord compression above L1 cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: compression of the cord = UMN; roots = LMN.

points.p: Hyperreflexia
points.why: UMN sign below the lesion.

points.p: Spasticity / increased tone
points.why: May be flaccid at first in acute compression.

points.p: Extensor plantars (Babinski)
points.why: Babinski with perianal sensory loss suggests a higher lesion.

points.p: Sensory level
points.why: Usually a few segments below the actual lesion.

prompts.q: How do cauda equina, conus medullaris and disc herniation differ from cord compression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the level decides UMN, LMN or mixed.

points.p: Cauda equina: LMN, saddle anaesthesia, retention, reduced anal tone, bilateral sciatica
points.why: Roots below the conus.

points.p: Conus medullaris (L1): mixed UMN and LMN
points.why: Absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars.

points.p: Disc herniation: acute unilateral pain and tingling, mostly L5/S1
points.why: Large central discs can cause cauda equina.

points.p: Epidural haematoma: anticoagulation or dural puncture
points.why: Rapidly rising pressure in a closed canal.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: whole spine, within 24 hours, steroids before the scan.

points.p: MRI whole spine
points.why: Metastases are often multilevel.

points.p: Within 24 hours
points.why: NICE CG75.

points.p: Then referral to neurosurgery / spinal team
points.why: Do not wait for results to call.

points.p: CT if MRI unavailable or contraindicated; plus bloods
points.why: For example a non-MRI-compatible pacemaker.

points.p: Dexamethasone before investigations if MSCC suspected
points.why: Never delay steroids for the scan.

prompts.q: What is the initial drug management of suspected MSCC, with doses?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: numbers matter: 16 STAT, 8 BD, plus stomach protection.

points.p: Dexamethasone 16 mg PO or IV STAT
points.why: Given before investigations.

points.p: Maintenance 8 mg BD
points.why: Continued until definitive treatment, then tapered.

points.p: PPI to prevent steroid-induced peptic ulceration
points.why: Also monitor glucose on high-dose steroids.

prompts.q: What is the definitive and emergency management of spinal cord compression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fit for surgery = decompression; not fit = radiotherapy; always escalate.

points.p: Surgical decompression after stabilisation with steroids
points.why: Definitive treatment.

points.p: Radiotherapy if unable to have surgery
points.why: Common in metastatic disease.

points.p: Urgent referral to acute oncology / neurosurgery
points.why: Same-day emergency.

points.p: Treat cause: antibiotics for abscess, surgery for disc
points.why: Epidural abscess: fever, back pain, neuro deficit, IVDU.

prompts.q: What long-term complications can spinal cord compression leave?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: think motor, sensory, sphincters and pain.

points.p: Permanent paralysis and loss of mobility
points.why: Function at diagnosis predicts outcome.

points.p: Permanent bladder and bowel dysfunction
points.why: Retention needs catheterisation.

points.p: Chronic neuropathic pain and sexual dysfunction
points.why: Needs long-term rehabilitation input.

prompts.q: Why does compression above L1 give UMN signs but cauda equina give LMN signs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the cord ends at about L1; below that are only roots.

points.p: Above the conus (about L1) the cord contains corticospinal tract fibres
points.why: Damage to descending fibres = UMN signs below.

points.p: Cauda equina is lumbosacral nerve roots (peripheral nerves) below the conus
points.why: Peripheral nerve damage = LMN signs.

points.p: LMN: reduced reflexes, flaccid weakness, saddle anaesthesia
points.why: The opposite of UMN findings.

prompts.q: Why are steroids and speed so important in metastatic cord compression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: oedema is reversible; ischaemia is not.

points.p: Vertebral body metastasis extends into the epidural space
points.why: Prostate, breast, lung, myeloma.

points.p: Venous congestion, oedema and direct compression
points.why: Early oedema is steroid-responsive.

points.p: Delay causes irreversible ischaemic cord injury
points.why: Why steroids are given before the scan.

glossary.MSCC: Metastatic spinal cord compression: cancer spread to the spine pressing on the spinal cord.
glossary.Cauda equina: The bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord, resembling a horse's tail.
glossary.Cauda equina syndrome: Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, retention and LMN leg signs.
glossary.Conus medullaris: The tapered lower end of the spinal cord, at about the L1 vertebra.
glossary.UMN: Upper motor neurone: damage to the brain or cord gives spasticity, brisk reflexes and extensor plantars.
glossary.LMN: Lower motor neurone: damage to roots or nerves gives flaccid weakness, wasting and reduced reflexes.
glossary.Corticospinal tract: The main motor pathway running from the cortex down the spinal cord to the motor neurones.
glossary.Babinski sign: Big toe extends upwards when the sole is stroked: an UMN sign.
glossary.Extensor plantars: An upgoing big toe on stroking the sole (Babinski sign), showing an upper motor neurone lesion.
glossary.Hyperreflexia: Exaggerated, brisk tendon reflexes: an upper motor neurone sign.
glossary.Spasticity: Velocity-dependent increased muscle tone from an upper motor neurone lesion.
glossary.Sensory level: A horizontal line on the body below which sensation is reduced, marking a cord lesion.
glossary.Saddle anaesthesia: Numbness of the perineum, buttocks and inner thighs, as in cauda equina syndrome.
glossary.Anal tone: Resting tightness of the anal sphincter on rectal examination; reduced in cauda equina.
glossary.Radicular pain: Pain shooting along the territory of a nerve root.
glossary.Sciatica: Pain radiating down the back of the leg from irritation of the L5 or S1 roots.
glossary.Urinary retention: Inability to empty the bladder; painless retention suggests a neurological cause.
glossary.Epidural space: The space between the vertebrae and the dura, containing fat and veins.
glossary.Epidural abscess: A collection of pus in the epidural space that can compress the cord; risk in IVDU.
glossary.Epidural haematoma: Bleeding into the epidural space, linked to anticoagulants or dural puncture.
glossary.Dural puncture: A needle breaching the dura, as in spinal anaesthesia or lumbar puncture.
glossary.IVDU: Intravenous drug use: a risk factor for epidural abscess and other bloodborne infections.
glossary.Disc prolapse: The soft centre of an intervertebral disc bulging through its outer ring onto nerves.
glossary.Vertebral collapse: Loss of height of a vertebral body, often from metastasis or osteoporosis.
glossary.Myeloma: A cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow causing lytic bone lesions, anaemia and hypercalcaemia.
glossary.Dexamethasone: A potent corticosteroid that reduces oedema around tumours compressing the cord.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, such as omeprazole, which reduces stomach acid and protects against ulcers.
glossary.Surgical decompression: An operation to remove tumour, bone or disc pressing on the cord or roots.
glossary.Radiotherapy: High-energy radiation used to shrink tumours; used if surgery is not possible.
glossary.Acute oncology: The hospital team that manages emergencies in patients with cancer.
glossary.MRC grade: Muscle power scale from 0 (no movement) to 5 (normal power).
glossary.Paraplegia: Paralysis of both legs, usually from a spinal cord lesion.
glossary.Neuropathic pain: Burning or shooting pain caused by damage to nerves themselves.
glossary.PSA: Prostate-specific antigen: a blood marker that is often very high in metastatic prostate cancer.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase: an enzyme that rises with bone metastases or liver disease.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 3 week history of severe thoracic back pain that wakes her at night. For 2 days her legs have felt weak and she has had difficulty passing urine. She had breast cancer treated 5 years ago. There is a sensory level at T8, brisk knee reflexes and extensor plantar responses. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: back pain plus neurology in a patient with a cancer history.

clues: thoracic back pain that wakes her at night
steps.x: Night thoracic pain, leg weakness, bladder symptoms, **UMN signs** with a sensory level, and a primary that spreads to bone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metastatic spinal cord compression** at the thoracic level.

elim: Cauda equina gives LMN signs and saddle anaesthesia, not brisk reflexes and a T8 level.
GBS gives ascending weakness with **absent** reflexes and no sensory level.
MS causes relapsing episodes, not progressive night pain in a cancer patient.
An osteoporotic fracture causes pain but not usually progressive cord signs; the cancer history matters more.

steps.x: **C. Metastatic spinal cord compression.** Rule: cancer + back pain + UMN signs = MSCC.

elim: CT thorax looks at the lungs, not the cord.

steps.x: **D. MRI whole spine.** Rule: MSCC is multilevel, so image the whole spine within 24 h.

elim: Zoledronic acid treats hypercalcaemia and bone pain, not cord compression.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man has a 2 day history of severe low back pain after lifting, with numbness around his anus and difficulty passing urine. Examination shows reduced power in ankle plantarflexion, absent ankle reflexes and reduced anal tone. Plantar responses are flexor.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his absent reflexes?
o: Compression of corticospinal tract fibres in the thoracic cord
Compression of lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris
Ischaemia of the anterior spinal artery

steps.x: Mechanism: why are the reflexes lost?
Saddle anaesthesia, retention and **LMN signs**: cauda equina syndrome from a disc.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Compression of **nerve roots** (peripheral nerves) below the conus = LMN.

elim: Corticospinal compression gives UMN signs: brisk reflexes, extensor plantars.
Dorsal column loss affects proprioception and vibration, not reflexes and sphincters this way.
Anterior spinal artery ischaemia is sudden and involves the cord (UMN later).
A cortical lesion gives UMN signs.

steps.x: **B. Compression of lumbosacral nerve roots.** Rule: cauda equina = roots = LMN.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has a 2 week history of severe mid-back pain at night and 3 days of progressive weakness of both legs. He has prostate cancer with bone metastases. There is a sensory level at T9, increased tone in both legs and extensor plantar responses. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 144/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Known bone metastases, night back pain and UMN signs with a sensory level is metastatic cord compression. Cauda equina gives LMN signs.

steps.x: Diagnosis: cancer patient with back pain and leg weakness.
MSCC red flags with **UMN signs** at a thoracic level.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metastatic spinal cord compression**.

elim: Cauda equina is LMN with saddle anaesthesia; this is UMN with a T9 level.
GBS gives areflexia with no sensory level.
Hypercalcaemia causes confusion and constipation, not a sensory level.
A hip fracture follows a fall and gives one painful, shortened leg.

steps.x: **D. Metastatic spinal cord compression.** Rule: cancer + back pain + UMN = MSCC.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has a 10 day history of thoracic back pain and 2 days of leg weakness. MRI shows spinal cord compression at T7. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 130/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her legs?
practice.e: Cord compression above L1 gives UMN signs below the lesion: extensor plantars, brisk reflexes and spasticity.

steps.x: Finding on examination for a cord lesion at T7.
Cord (not roots) compressed well above L1.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **UMN signs**: extensor plantars.

elim: Absent ankle reflexes are LMN (cauda equina or neuropathy).
Fasciculations are LMN (e.g. MND).
Flaccid tone with wasting is LMN and chronic.
Saddle anaesthesia alone fits cauda equina.

steps.x: **B. Extensor plantar responses.** Rule: cord above L1 = UMN signs below.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man has a 1 day history of severe low back pain radiating down both legs after moving furniture. He has not passed urine for 12 hours and has numbness around his buttocks and perineum. Ankle reflexes are absent and anal tone is reduced. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, retention and reduced anal tone after lifting is cauda equina syndrome from a central disc prolapse.

steps.x: Diagnosis of back pain with neurological features.

clues: numbness around his buttocks and perineum
steps.x: Bilateral sciatica, retention, **saddle anaesthesia**, LMN signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cauda equina syndrome**.

elim: Mechanical pain has no neurology or sphincter loss.
MSCC needs cancer and gives UMN signs above L1.
Spinal stenosis causes chronic claudication-like leg pain on walking.
Pain is in both legs with sphincter loss: more than simple sciatica.

steps.x: **A. Cauda equina syndrome.** Rule: saddle anaesthesia + retention + LMN = cauda equina.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man who injects heroin has a 5 day history of severe thoracic back pain and fever. Today he cannot stand. There is tenderness over T6 and a sensory level at T8. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his cord compression?
practice.e: Fever, back pain, neurological deficit and IVDU with very high inflammatory markers is a spinal epidural abscess.

steps.x: Cause of cord compression.

clues: severe thoracic back pain and fever
steps.x: Epidural abscess red flags: **fever, back pain, neuro deficit, IVDU**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Epidural abscess**.

elim: Disc prolapse is lumbar, after lifting, without fever.
Haematoma needs anticoagulation or dural puncture.
No known cancer; fever and a CRP of 246 point to infection.
Osteoporotic collapse is in older people without fever.

steps.x: **B. Epidural abscess.** Rule: fever + back pain + neurology + IVDU = abscess.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has a 2 month history of back pain and tiredness, and 2 days of leg weakness with a sensory level at T11. He has no previous history of cancer. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his cord compression?
practice.e: Anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and high total protein with bone pain is multiple myeloma, one of the four main causes of MSCC.

steps.x: Underlying cause; look hard at the bloods.

clues: leg weakness with a sensory level at T11
steps.x: Bloods: low Hb, high calcium, high creatinine, high protein and ESR: **CRAB** features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Multiple myeloma** with vertebral involvement.

elim: No fever; abscess gives a high CRP and WCC, not high protein and calcium.
Disc prolapse does not cause anaemia or hypercalcaemia.
Spinal TB gives fever, night sweats and weight loss, not hypercalcaemia with high protein.
Haemangiomas are benign and do not cause these bloods.

steps.x: **C. Multiple myeloma.** Rule: back pain + CRAB bloods = myeloma, a classic MSCC primary.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman with atrial fibrillation takes apixaban. She develops sudden severe back pain followed within 3 hours by weakness of both legs and urinary retention. There is a sensory level at T10. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 168/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her cord compression?
practice.e: Sudden back pain then rapid cord signs in an anticoagulated patient is a spinal epidural haematoma: a neurosurgical emergency.

steps.x: Cause of an acute cord compression.
Anticoagulated, **sudden** pain then rapid deficit: bleeding into a closed canal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Spinal epidural haematoma**.

elim: Anterior spinal artery infarction is ischaemia, not compression, and spares proprioception; anticoagulation points to bleeding.
Disc prolapse is mostly lumbar, after lifting.
No fever or infection risk.
No known cancer and the onset is too fast.

steps.x: **E. Spinal epidural haematoma.** Rule: anticoagulant + sudden pain + rapid cord signs = haematoma.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has an MRI showing a single-level cord compression at T6. She was given dexamethasone 16 mg yesterday. She is otherwise well and fit for surgery, with a good prognosis. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: After steroid stabilisation, surgical decompression is definitive in a fit patient. Radiotherapy is used if surgery is not possible.

steps.x: Definitive management.
Stabilised with steroids and fit: the best option is surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Surgical decompression**, usually followed by radiotherapy.

elim: Chemotherapy is too slow to relieve compression.
Steroids only bridge to definitive treatment.
Physiotherapy is rehabilitation, not decompression.
Radiotherapy alone is for those who cannot have surgery.

steps.x: **E. Surgical decompression.** Rule: steroids first, then surgery if fit.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer and suspected cord compression is given dexamethasone 16 mg STAT and prescribed 8 mg twice daily. He has a past history of a duodenal ulcer.
practice.e: A PPI is added prophylactically to protect against steroid-induced peptic ulceration.

steps.x: Which drug goes with high-dose dexamethasone?
High-dose steroids and an ulcer history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **PPI**: omeprazole.

elim: Alendronate protects bone long term; it does not protect the stomach.
Calcium does not prevent ulcers.
Metoclopramide is an antiemetic.
Senna treats constipation.

steps.x: **D. Omeprazole.** Rule: dexamethasone in MSCC always comes with a PPI.

practice.stem: An 82 year old man with metastatic lung cancer, severe COPD and heart failure has MRI-confirmed cord compression at T4 and T10. He has received dexamethasone. The spinal surgeons say he is not fit for surgery. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
practice.e: When surgery is not possible, radiotherapy is the definitive treatment for MSCC.

steps.x: Definitive treatment when surgery is off the table.
Unfit, multilevel disease, steroids given.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Radiotherapy**.

elim: Bisphosphonates help bone pain and calcium, not compression.
Steroids are a bridge, not definitive.
Laminectomy is surgery, which he cannot have.
Physiotherapy does not decompress the cord.

steps.x: **E. Radiotherapy.** Rule: unfit for surgery = radiotherapy.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with breast cancer has MRI-confirmed compression of the spinal cord at T8. She has brisk knee and ankle reflexes, increased tone and extensor plantar responses in both legs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the brisk reflexes?
o: Compression of corticospinal tract fibres above the conus medullaris
Damage to anterior horn cells at T8
practice.e: Compression above the conus (about L1) damages corticospinal tract fibres heading to lower levels, giving UMN signs below the lesion.

steps.x: Mechanism: why are the reflexes brisk?

clues: compression of the spinal cord at T8
steps.x: Cord lesion at T8 with **UMN** signs below it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Loss of descending **corticospinal** inhibition below the lesion.

elim: Root compression gives LMN signs (reduced reflexes).
Anterior horn damage at T8 gives LMN signs at that segment only.
DRG inflammation affects sensation, not reflex briskness.
Peripheral neuropathy reduces reflexes.

steps.x: **A. Corticospinal tract compression.** Rule: cord above L1 = UMN signs below.
